why.correct: The boxes show 2 N₂ and 6 H₂ becoming 4 NH₃. Dividing by 2 gives the smallest whole-number ratio, 1 : 3 : 2, so N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. Each side has 2 N and 6 H.
options: Right: 2 N and 6 H on each side, in the smallest whole-number ratio.
Unbalanced: 2 N and 2 H on the left but 1 N and 3 H on the right, so atoms would appear and vanish.
Changes the formula of ammonia to NH₆ to make the atoms fit. Subscripts are fixed by what the substance is; only coefficients may change.
Writes nitrogen and hydrogen as single atoms, but the diagram shows them as two-atom molecules, N₂ and H₂.

why.correct: Four NH₃ molecules × 3 H atoms each = 12 H atoms, the same as the 6 H₂ × 2 = 12 H atoms before. Atoms are conserved.
Atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed, so the number of each kind of atom and the total mass stay the same. The molecules themselves change, and so does their count (8 before, 4 after).
options: Right: 4 N atoms before and 4 after.
There are 8 molecules before and 4 after. Molecules are not conserved; atoms are.
Right: the same atoms are present, so the mass is the same.
N₂ and H₂ are replaced by NH₃: new substances form, which is what makes this a reaction.

why.correct: Count atoms, not molecules: 4 N + 12 H = 16 atoms before and 16 after. The atoms regrouped into four larger molecules.
options: Right: the same 16 atoms are there in fewer, larger molecules.
Ordinary reactions do not turn measurable mass into energy; every atom is still in the box.
Every hydrogen atom from the Before box is inside an NH₃ molecule after; none is missing.
Molecules are not the unit that is conserved; atoms are, and their number is unchanged.

why.correct: 148.62 g − 147.58 g = 1.04 g. When you subtract, keep the decimal places of the measurements (two here), which gives three significant figures.

In the capped bottle, nothing could leave and the mass did not change. The open flask lost 1.04 g because the gas product (carbon dioxide) left the flask. Both trials agree with conservation of mass once every product is counted.
options: Right: the capped trial shows no change; the open trial lost only the escaping gas.
Whether a flask is open cannot change whether matter is conserved; it changes whether a product can leave the balance.
The cap was on the bottle for both weighings in Trial 2, so it adds the same mass before and after.
Trial 1 did not weigh all the products: the gas left. Trial 2, which kept everything, shows no difference.

why.correct: A gas forming without boiling suggests a new substance is being made. A smell noticed before mixing describes a reactant, a solid disappearing into a liquid can be just dissolving, and an unchanged color is not evidence of anything.
options: Right: gas forms at room temperature, so it is not boiling; a new substance is being made.
That describes the vinegar before anything happened, so it says nothing about a change.
Sugar also disappears into water without forming anything new; dissolving alone does not show a reaction.
No change in color is not evidence of a reaction.

why.correct: A leak lets some carbon dioxide out, so the balance no longer weighs every product and the reading drops below the true total.
options: Right: the gas that leaks out is no longer weighed.
The gas inside is under higher pressure than the air outside, so gas flows out, not in; the escaping gas lowers the reading.
Trial 1 shows that the escaping gas weighs about 1 g, which a balance reading to 0.01 g detects easily.
A reaction rearranges atoms; it does not use up matter. The drop comes from gas leaving.

why.correct: Oxygen comes in pairs on the left and threes on the right, so make 6 O on each side: 3 O₂ and 2 Al₂O₃. Then 2 Al₂O₃ holds 4 Al, so 4 Al. Check: 4 Al, 6 O on both sides.
options: Right: 4 Al and 6 O on each side.
Gives 2 Al and 6 O on the left but 2 Al and 3 O on the right; oxygen does not balance.
Gives 2 O on the left and 3 O on the right; oxygen does not balance.
Balances, but every coefficient can be halved; equations use the smallest whole-number ratio.

why.correct: The right side has 3 × 2 = 6 O in CO₂ and 4 × 1 = 4 O in H₂O, 10 O in all. Ten O atoms are 5 O₂ molecules.
options: Right: 10 O atoms on the right, so 5 O₂.
Adds the coefficients 3 + 4; the oxygen atoms in each formula must be counted.
That is the number of O atoms needed; O₂ carries two per molecule, so half as many molecules.
Counts only the oxygen in CO₂ molecules, not their atoms, and ignores the water.

why.correct: A subscript is part of what the substance is: H₂O is water and H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide. Balance with coefficients: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.
options: Right: changing a subscript changes the substance; 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O is the balanced equation.
The atoms do balance, but the equation now describes making hydrogen peroxide, not water.
Oxygen exists as O₂ molecules; writing a lone O atom changes the reactant.
Changing a subscript on either side changes the substance, so it is not allowed anywhere.

why.correct: Coefficients count particles, so they also count moles (a mole is just a fixed number of particles). They do not give masses: 2 mol H₂ is 4.03 g and 1 mol O₂ is 32.00 g.
options: Right: coefficients are counts of particles, and so of moles.
Coefficients are not mass ratios; 2 mol of H₂ (4.03 g) is far lighter than 1 mol of O₂ (32.00 g).
Coefficients are not grams; molar masses differ.
The coefficient 2 counts H₂ molecules, not H atoms: 2 H₂ hold 4 H atoms, so 4 H atoms react with each O₂ molecule.

why.correct: Mass is conserved: 4.86 g + 3.20 g = 8.06 g of MgO. Adding keeps two decimal places.
Bubbles in boiling water are water vapor, the same substance in another state. No new substance forms. The other three point to a new substance with new properties.
options: Right: boiling makes bubbles of water vapor, not a new substance.
A color change when a metal is added suggests a new substance forms, so it is stronger evidence.
A new solid forming from two solutions is strong evidence of a new substance.
A new smell suggests a new substance, so it is stronger evidence than boiling.

why.correct: Formulas first (they are fixed), then count, then adjust coefficients, then simplify and check the count once more.
2Fe + 3Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃: chlorine comes in twos and threes, so make 6 Cl on each side (3 Cl₂ and 2 FeCl₃), then 2 Fe. The sum is 2 + 3 + 2 = 7.
Pb²⁺ needs two NO₃⁻ and two I⁻, and K⁺ pairs with one NO₃⁻. Treat NO₃ as one unit: 1 Pb, 2 NO₃, 2 K, 2 I on each side.
options: Right: every unit balances, and each formula matches the ion charges.
Leaves 1 K and 1 I on the left but 2 I on the right, and 2 NO₃ on the left but 1 on the right.
Writes formulas that do not match the charges: lead here is Pb²⁺, so it pairs with two nitrates and two iodides.
K₂(NO₃)₂ is not a formula unit; potassium nitrate is KNO₃, and balancing uses a coefficient.

why.correct: Dissolving breaks attractions between ions and forms ion-dipole attractions with water, which can warm or cool the water, yet the ions are the same before and after. Proof of a reaction is a new substance.
options: Right: dissolving alone can warm or cool water.
Dissolving and phase changes also change temperature, so a temperature change is not reliable proof by itself.
Many reactions involve solids in water without melting, such as a metal dissolving in acid.
A thermometer can measure the change; the problem is what the change means, not its size.

why.correct: Only silver and chloride ions change: they go from moving separately in water to a packed solid. Sodium and nitrate ions look the same before and after, so they are left out.
options: Right: the only species that change are Ag⁺ and Cl⁻, which form solid AgCl.
Sodium and nitrate ions are still separate in the water after mixing, so no NaNO₃ solid forms.
This is the molecular equation. It is balanced, but it shows spectators and treats dissolved ionic compounds as if they were intact units.
The solid is the compound AgCl, held together by attraction between oppositely charged ions; it is written as one formula with no charges.

why.correct: A spectator ion is in the solution, unchanged, before and after. Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ are still free in the water after mixing.
options: Right: sodium ions start and end dissolved in the water.
Right: nitrate ions start and end dissolved in the water.
Silver ions leave the solution and become part of the solid, so they take part.
Chloride ions leave the solution and become part of the solid, so they take part.

why.correct: Three Na⁺ and three NO₃⁻ remain in the water: 6 ions. The six Ag⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are in the solid.
The spectator ions stay in solution and pass through the filter paper. If the water evaporates, they pack together as solid sodium nitrate.
options: Right: the spectators stay dissolved and pass through.
The filter paper holds back the solid; it does not break it into ions.
Sodium and nitrate ions never left the solution; only silver and chloride did.
No electrons are transferred here; sodium and chloride stay as ions throughout.

why.correct: K⁺ and NO₃⁻ are spectators (their compounds are soluble). The yellow solid must be lead(II) iodide. Pb²⁺ needs two I⁻ to make a neutral solid, and the charges balance: +2 + 2(−1) = 0 on the left, 0 on the right.
options: Right: atoms and charges both balance, and only the changing species appear.
PbI would need lead to be +1. With Pb²⁺, the neutral solid is PbI₂, and the left side carries a +1 charge that the right side lacks.
Potassium nitrate is soluble, so its ions stay dissolved; they are the spectators.
This is the molecular equation, which includes the spectator ions in its formulas.

why.correct: Mixing the solutions only gives a solution of four kinds of ions, K⁺, Cl⁻, Na⁺ and NO₃⁻, all spectators. Nothing changes, so there is no net ionic equation (no reaction).
options: Right: all four ions are spectators.
KNO₃(aq) is just K⁺ and NO₃⁻ dissolved, the same as before; nothing has changed.
Every possible combination is soluble according to the data given, so no solid can form.
At 0.1 M the ions meet constantly; wells 1, 2 and 4 react at the same concentration.

why.correct: Sodium compounds are soluble, so Na⁺ and SO₄²⁻ stay in solution. The blue solid is copper(II) hydroxide; Cu²⁺ needs two OH⁻.
options: Right: atoms and charge balance and only the changing ions appear.
With Cu²⁺, one OH⁻ leaves a +1 charge; the neutral solid needs two hydroxide ions.
Sodium sulfate is soluble (all sodium compounds are), and its formula would be Na₂SO₄ in any case.
The reactants are dissolved, not solids; writing (s) for them misdescribes the solutions in the wells.

why.correct: A solid forms only when a combination of ions cannot stay dissolved. In well 2 the new combinations are BaSO₄ and NaCl; NaCl is soluble, so the white solid is BaSO₄. In well 1 the yellow solid is PbI₂.
options: Right: the white solid in well 2 must be barium sulfate.
Right: the yellow solid in well 1 must be lead(II) iodide.
All sodium compounds are soluble, and well 3 shows Na⁺ and Cl⁻ staying in solution.
All nitrate and potassium compounds are soluble, as the note says.

why.correct: The solid stays as a formula because its ions are locked in the solid, not free in water. HCl is fully ionized, so it appears as H⁺ with Cl⁻ as a spectator. Ca²⁺ ends up dissolved and must appear as a product.
options: Right: the solid is written whole, Cl⁻ is dropped, and charge balances (+2 each side).
Splits a solid into ions. A solid is written as a formula because its ions are not free in solution.
Leaves out the solid entirely and treats it as if carbonate ions were already dissolved.
This is the molecular equation; HCl and CaCl₂ are dissolved as ions and Cl⁻ is a spectator.

why.correct: A net ionic equation balances atoms and charge. Here the charges are +1 and +2. With 2Ag⁺ and 2Ag both balance: Zn(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s).
options: Right: the charge is unbalanced; 2Ag⁺ and 2Ag fix it.
Atoms balance, but charge does not; both must balance.
Zinc starts as a solid metal, so it is written Zn(s).
Charge is conserved, so the total charge must match on both sides.

why.correct: A dissolved ionic compound separates into its ions. Polyatomic ions such as sulfate stay together. Two Na⁺ balance one SO₄²⁻.
options: Right: two sodium ions and one intact sulfate ion.
The subscript 2 means two separate Na⁺ ions, each +1; there is no Na₂⁺ ion.
Sulfate is a polyatomic ion held by covalent bonds; it does not fall apart in water.
In a complete ionic equation a dissolved ionic compound is written as its separate ions.

why.correct: Left side: 2Ag⁺ + 2NO₃⁻ + Ca²⁺ + 2Cl⁻. The spectators are the 2 NO₃⁻ and the 1 Ca²⁺, which reappear unchanged on the right: 3 ions. The net ionic equation is Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s).
Write each species the way most of it exists in the solution. A weak electrolyte is mostly un-ionized molecules, so it is written as its formula with (aq).
options: Right: write the form that dominates in the solution.
Only strong electrolytes, which separate almost completely, are written as ions.
In the solution it is dissolved, so (aq); (l) is for a pure liquid.
Acetic acid itself reacts in such equations, so it appears; a spectator is something unchanged on both sides.

why.correct: Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s) describes mixing silver nitrate with sodium chloride, potassium chloride or calcium chloride: the spectators differ, but the change is the same.
options: Right: it shows the change itself, whatever the spectators are.
That is the complete ionic equation; the net ionic equation removes the spectators.
Water appears only when it is a reactant or product.
No equation gives masses directly; the coefficients count particles.

why.correct: Only Ag⁺ and Cl⁻ react. Sodium ions accumulate as spectators, nitrate ions stay put, and the solid grows.

variables.name: Number of dissolved Ag⁺ ions
variables.why: Silver ions join chloride ions in the solid, so fewer remain dissolved.

variables.name: Number of dissolved NO₃⁻ ions
variables.why: Nitrate is a spectator: it neither joins the solid nor is added, so the count is unchanged.

variables.name: Number of dissolved Na⁺ ions
variables.why: Each drop of NaCl(aq) adds sodium ions, which stay dissolved as spectators.

variables.name: Mass of solid in the beaker
variables.why: AgCl forms as a solid, so solid mass grows as silver ions are used.

why.correct: NaCl(aq) means Na⁺ and Cl⁻ dissolved in water, exactly the left side. No new substance forms, so no reaction is shown.
options: Right: both sides are the same dissolved ions.
Dividing by 2 still leaves an equation that shows no change.
Sodium chloride is soluble, so in water it is dissolved ions, not a solid.
A chloride ion is Cl⁻; the charges in the equation are correct.

why.correct: Two O₂ molecules were used (3 before, 1 after) to turn 4 CO into 4 CO₂, a 4 : 2 : 4 ratio, which is 2 : 1 : 2. The leftover O₂ did not react, so it is not part of the equation.
options: Right: the ratio of what reacted, in smallest whole numbers.
Puts the unreacted O₂ on both sides. An equation shows what reacts in what ratio, not the leftover amount in one particular mixture.
Unbalanced: 3 O atoms on the left and 2 on the right.
Oxygen gas exists as O₂ molecules, as the diagram shows, not as single O atoms.

why.correct: The reactant left over is the one in excess. All four CO molecules were used; one O₂ remains.
options: Right: some O₂ is left unreacted.
Starting with more particles does not make a reactant the excess one; what matters is the ratio needed. Each O₂ handles two CO, so 3 O₂ could handle 6 CO.
CO₂ is a product, not a reactant.
Atoms are always conserved, but that does not mean both reactants were used up.

why.correct: Three O₂ need 3 × 2 = 6 CO. The box has 4, so add 2 more. Equivalently, the one leftover O₂ needs 2 CO.
Count: 4 CO + 3 O₂ = 7 molecules before; 4 CO₂ + 1 O₂ = 5 after. The equation 2CO + O₂ → 2CO₂ turns 3 gas molecules into 2.
options: Right: 7 molecules become 5.
Atoms are conserved, but molecules are not; atoms regroup into fewer, larger molecules.
The number of molecules, not their size, is what is counted, and that number goes down.
All atoms stay in gas molecules, as the After box shows; none leave the gas.

why.correct: Used: 2 X₂ (3 before, 1 after) and 6 Y₂, making 4 XY₃. The ratio 2 : 6 : 4 reduces to 1 : 3 : 2.
options: Right: the reacting ratio in smallest whole numbers.
Includes the leftover X₂ on both sides; leave unreacted particles out of the equation.
The elements are drawn as two-atom molecules, X₂ and Y₂.
Balanced, and the right ratio, but every coefficient can be halved.

why.correct: The limiting reactant is the one that runs out. No Y₂ remains, while one X₂ does; Y₂ ran out first.
options: Right: Y₂ is used up, so it sets how much product forms.
Fewer particles does not mean limiting; each X₂ needs three Y₂, so X₂ goes further.
A leftover reactant is the one in excess, the opposite of limiting.
There are 6 X atoms and 12 Y atoms, which are not equal; in any case the ratio needed (1 : 3), not equality, decides.

why.correct: For 5 X₂ you would need 15 Y₂; there are only 9, so Y₂ limits. 9 Y₂ × (2 XY₃ / 3 Y₂) = 6 XY₃. Check atoms: 6 XY₃ hold 6 X and 18 Y; 3 X₂ are used and 2 X₂ are left.
There are 6 X and 12 Y atoms in each box. The molecules regroup (9 before, 5 after), so molecule counts need not match; atom counts must.
options: Right: atoms are conserved, so each kind of atom is counted the same in both boxes.
There are 9 molecules before and 5 after; molecules are not conserved.
Particles do not pair off one-to-one; here 1 X₂ and 3 Y₂ make 2 XY₃, as the coefficients say.
The coefficients, not a rule of equality, set how many of each appear.

why.correct: Melted salt is a pure liquid, so (l). (aq) would mean dissolved in water, and there is no water here.
options: Right: a melted pure substance is a liquid.
(aq) means dissolved in water; melted salt contains no water.
(s) is the salt before it melts.
Salt does not boil until far above its melting point; at this stage it is a liquid.

why.correct: The state symbol tells how the product exists. The atoms and coefficients are unchanged; the water is gas instead of liquid, which matters later for energy.
options: Right: same atoms and ratio; water as vapor.
The reactants are unchanged; only the state of the product differs.
The coefficients, not the state symbol, set how many molecules form.
State symbols carry meaning: liquid water and water vapor are different states of the same substance.

why.correct: NaCl(s) is an ionic solid: a lattice of alternating cations and anions packed close together. There are no separate molecules.
options: Right: an ionic solid is an extended array of alternating ions.
Ionic compounds do not form discrete molecules; the formula NaCl is a ratio of ions.
In the product the elements are ions held together, not separate neutral atoms.
That shows NaCl(aq); the equation says (s) and there is no water.

why.correct: 12 H₂ need 12 ÷ 3 = 4 N₂. There are 6 N₂, so H₂ runs out first and 6 − 4 = 2 N₂ molecules are left. 8 NH₃ form.

4 SO₂ + 2 O₂ = 4 S and 12 O before. 4 SO₃ + 1 O₂ = 4 S and 14 O after: two oxygen atoms appeared. 4 SO₂ and 2 O₂ are in the exact 2 : 1 ratio, so both should be used up, giving 4 SO₃ and nothing else.
options: Right: 12 O atoms before, 14 after.
Right: the reactants are in the exact ratio, so no O₂ should remain.
4 SO₂ make 4 SO₃, which is the right number.
There are 4 S atoms in each box.

why.correct: Ratio 6 : 6 : 3 reduces to 2 : 2 : 1. Check: 2 A and 4 B on each side.
options: Right: the counts reduce to 2 : 2 : 1 and atoms balance.
The diagram shows B leaving as B₂ molecules, not single atoms.
Adds a molecule that is not in the diagram and keeps the large counts.
The diagram shows AB molecules, not separate A atoms, as a product.

why.correct: Three CH₄ would need 6 O₂; there are only 4, so O₂ is limiting. 4 O₂ react with 2 CH₄ and make 2 CO₂ and 4 H₂O; 1 CH₄ is left. Atom check: 3 C, 12 H and 8 O in both lists.
options: Right: O₂ runs out, leaving one CH₄; atoms balance.
Uses all the CH₄ as if O₂ were plentiful; that would need 6 O₂ and creates oxygen atoms.
Treats CH₄ as limiting, but 4 O₂ are not enough for 3 CH₄; this list also has too few carbon atoms.
Forgets the coefficient 2 on water: each CH₄ gives two H₂O, so hydrogen atoms go missing.

why.correct: In P and R the molecules after are different from the molecules before: bonds broke and new ones formed. In Q every Br₂ molecule is intact; only the arrangement of the molecules changed.
options: Right: new substances form in P and R.
Q is the one change in which every molecule stays the same, so it is the physical change.
Q keeps the same Br₂ molecules, so it is not a chemical change.
P also makes new substances (H₂ and O₂ from water).

why.correct: The molecules end up far apart but each is still Br₂. Only the forces between molecules were overcome: a phase change, which is physical.
options: Right: the molecules separate, but each molecule stays whole.
The second box still shows Br₂ pairs, so no Br–Br bond broke.
No new compound appears; every particle is still Br₂.
No ions appear in the diagram, and there is no water to dissolve in.

why.correct: 6 NO hold 6 O atoms and 3 O₂ hold 6 O atoms: 12 in all, matching the 6 NO₂ × 2 = 12 O atoms before.
Every reaction keeps the same atoms, so "same atoms" cannot tell physical from chemical. What matters is whether bonds within particles break and new ones form. In P they do.
options: Right: bonds inside the particles change, so new substances form.
Atoms are present before and after any change; that alone does not make a change physical.
Whether a change can be undone does not decide it; many chemical changes can be undone by another reaction.
A change of state alone is physical; P is chemical because new substances form, not because a gas appears.

why.correct: Boiling needs about 41 kJ/mol, while breaking the O–H bonds needs about 927 kJ/mol, over 20 times more. Boiling separates whole molecules; it does not break covalent bonds.
options: Right: the intermolecular attractions overcome in boiling are much weaker than covalent bonds.
Boiling separates whole molecules; no O–H bond breaks. 41 ÷ 927 is a ratio of energies, not a share of bonds broken.
Both processes need energy; that does not decide physical or chemical. Making H and O atoms from water is chemical, since new substances form.
The data show the opposite: 41 kJ/mol to separate molecules versus 927 kJ/mol to break bonds.

why.correct: 927 kJ/mol ÷ 41 kJ/mol = 22.6, which is 23 to the two significant figures of 41.
Condensing is the reverse of boiling: the same attractions between molecules form again, so the same 41 kJ/mol is released. No O–H bonds broke on boiling, so none re-form.
options: Right: forming intermolecular attractions releases the energy boiling took in.
No O–H bonds broke when the water boiled, so none re-form on condensing.
Physical changes involve energy too; boiling and condensing are examples.
Particles moving closer as attractions form release energy; separating them is what takes energy.

why.correct: Dissolving breaks the strong attractions between Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in the crystal, like breaking bonds, and forms ion-dipole attractions with water. Yet the ions are unchanged and evaporating the water returns the solid salt. It has features of both kinds of change.
options: Right: strong attractions break and new ones form, but the ions themselves are unchanged.
NaCl is held by ionic, not covalent, bonds, and the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions survive in the solution.
Dissolving does involve energy, like melting or boiling; the water can warm or cool as salt dissolves.
Dissolved salt is Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in water, not sodium metal and chlorine gas.

why.correct: Copper turning green forms new copper compounds; yeast converts sugar into carbon dioxide and ethanol. Dry ice subliming and sugar dissolving keep the same molecules.
options: Right: new copper compounds form on the surface.
Sublimation keeps CO₂ molecules whole; only their state changes.
Right: sugar molecules are turned into new substances.
Sugar molecules separate and mix with water but are still sugar molecules.

why.correct: Boiling is a physical change: water molecules escape the liquid as vapor. No O–H bonds break, so no H₂ or O₂ forms.
options: Right: the bubbles are water vapor.
Making H₂ and O₂ would need O–H bonds to break, a chemical change that takes far more energy than boiling.
A little dissolved air comes out when water is first heated, but the bubbles of a rolling boil are water vapor.
The bubbles hold water vapor at about 1 atm, pushing back on the liquid.

why.correct: In a phase change the particles are unchanged; only the distance between them and the attractions they feel change.

variables.name: Number of ethanol molecules
variables.why: Evaporation is physical: every ethanol molecule leaves the liquid intact, so the count is unchanged.

variables.name: Average distance between ethanol molecules
variables.why: Molecules in a gas are far apart, much farther than in the liquid.

variables.name: Total mass in the container
variables.why: Nothing enters or leaves the sealed container, so mass is unchanged.

variables.name: Number of C–O bonds
variables.why: No bonds within the molecules break in a phase change.

why.correct: The water in the blue crystals is bonded into the solid in a fixed ratio; removing it gives a different compound with a different color. That the reaction can be run backward does not make it physical.
options: Right: a compound of fixed composition lost a component and became a new substance.
Being able to undo a change does not make it physical; this is a chemical change run in both directions.
The water leaving was bonded into the crystal, so its loss makes a new substance with new properties.
Atoms are the same in every change; the substance present changed.

why.correct: Heating the white solid makes a gas and a solid with properties the starting material lacks. Iodine vapor and shrinking ice are the same substances changing state, and sugar crystallizing from syrup is sugar coming out of solution.
options: Right: a new gas and a new solid form.
Purple iodine vapor is I₂ molecules, the same as in the crystal.
Ice slowly turns directly to water vapor in a freezer; the molecules stay H₂O.
The crystals are the same sugar molecules that were dissolved; they come out of solution as it cools.

why.correct: Sublimation separates whole molecules; the covalent I–I bond stays intact because it is far stronger than the dispersion forces between molecules.
options: Right: intermolecular forces are overcome; the covalent bond is not.
If the bond were weaker, warming would split molecules into atoms before they left the solid.
A phase change does not break covalent bonds; the gas is I₂ molecules from the start.
Iodine is a solid at room temperature, so attractions between its molecules do hold it together.

why.correct: A pure substance keeps its melting point, so sample 1 is the same substance after melting and refreezing. Sample 2 released a gas and left a solid with a different melting point, so new substances formed.
options: Right: a new gas and a solid with a new melting point show new substances.
Heating can cause either kind of change; only sample 2 shows new substances.
Melting is a phase change; the unchanged melting point shows it is the same substance.
Color alone does not decide; the different melting point and the gas show sample 2 changed.

why.correct: Mass of AgCl = 23.3851 g − 22.4518 g = 0.9333 g (the last two dryings agree, so the solid is dry). 0.9333 g × (1 mol / 143.32 g) = 0.006512 mol AgCl, to four significant figures.
0.9333 g AgCl × (1 mol AgCl / 143.32 g) × (1 mol Cl / 1 mol AgCl) × (35.45 g / 1 mol Cl) = 0.2308 g Cl. 0.2308 g ÷ 0.5120 g × 100 = 45.09% chloride.
The solid weighed after drying 1 includes water, so the mass of "AgCl" is too large. That gives too many moles of Cl and a percent that is too high. Drying to constant mass removes this error.
options: Right: extra mass from water is counted as AgCl.
The calculation turns the whole mass into moles of AgCl, so extra water raises the result, not lowers it.
Water has no chloride, but its mass is wrongly counted as AgCl, which inflates the result.
Drying removes water, not AgCl; and losing AgCl would lower the result.

why.correct: The chloride in the sample must be the limiting reactant, so all of it ends up in the solid. A small excess of Ag⁺ makes sure of that. Extra Ag⁺ cannot make more AgCl than the chloride allows.
options: Right: an excess of silver ions makes chloride the limiting reactant.
The point is to keep the precipitate on the paper, not dissolve it.
Nitrate is a spectator ion; it does not react, so it is not a reactant at all.
Once all the chloride is used, more Ag⁺ makes no more AgCl; the excess stays dissolved.

why.correct: At 20.0 mL the mass is still rising with volume: beakers with more KI made more solid. So iodide runs out first there, and lead ions are left in excess. The mass stops rising only after about 40 mL.
options: Right: on the rising part of the graph, iodide is the limiting reactant.
The mass levels off near 40 mL, not at 20 mL; at 20 mL it is still rising.
Volume alone does not decide; it is the moles of each ion and the 1 : 2 ratio needed.
The ratio of the equation is fixed, but the amounts mixed are not; at 20 mL there are not enough I⁻ ions for every Pb²⁺.

why.correct: Where the graph is flat, all the Pb²⁺ has precipitated. 0.922 g ÷ 461.0 g/mol = 0.00200 mol PbI₂ = 0.00200 mol Pb²⁺ (1 : 1). 0.00200 mol ÷ 0.0250 L = 0.0800 M.

At the break, the two reactants are used up together. 0.0400 L × 0.100 mol/L = 0.00400 mol I⁻, and the lead found from the plateau is 0.00200 mol: a 2 : 1 ratio of I⁻ to Pb²⁺, as in Pb²⁺ + 2I⁻ → PbI₂.
options: Right: moles of iodide at the break are twice the moles of lead.
Volumes are not moles; the concentrations differ, so compare moles.
A 1 : 1 solid would level off at 20 mL, half the observed volume.
Before 40 mL iodide is limiting, not in excess; after 40 mL it is in excess.

why.correct: Past 40 mL, lead ions are the limiting reactant. Once they are used up, more iodide stays dissolved as an excess reactant and the mass of solid is fixed.
options: Right: the lead ions are used up.
The total volume does not limit the reaction; the amount of Pb²⁺ does.
The mass stays the same rather than falling, so the solid is not dissolving.
K⁺ is a spectator ion and does not stop the reaction.

why.correct: Mass of NaHCO₃ = 23.905 g − 21.385 g = 2.520 g. 2.520 g × (1 mol / 84.01 g) × (1 mol Na₂CO₃ / 2 mol NaHCO₃) × (105.99 g / 1 mol) = 1.590 g Na₂CO₃.
While the mass still drops, gas is still leaving and some NaHCO₃ has not decomposed. Agreement between heatings 2 and 3 (22.968 g and 22.967 g) shows the reaction has finished.
options: Right: a constant mass shows no more gas is leaving.
The crucible is chosen because it does not react or decompose.
The desiccator keeps the sample from picking up water from the air; absorbing water would spoil the data.
The readings are not averaged; the final constant mass is used, because the earlier ones are not of the finished product.

why.correct: Anything that leaves extra mass in the crucible raises the "actual yield". Undecomposed NaHCO₃ or absorbed water add mass. Spattering removes solid, lowering the yield. A hot crucible sets up air currents that make it read light, lowering the yield.
options: Right: undecomposed NaHCO₃ is still there and counted as product.
Right: water picked up from the air adds mass that is counted as product.
Solid that spatters out is lost, so the actual yield is too low.
Rising warm air makes a hot crucible read lighter, so the yield would come out too low.

why.correct: 10.0 g × (1 mol C₃H₈ / 44.09 g) × (5 mol O₂ / 1 mol C₃H₈) × (32.00 g / 1 mol O₂) = 36.3 g O₂.

N₂: 20.0 g ÷ 28.02 g/mol = 0.7138 mol, which could make 1.428 mol NH₃. H₂: 5.00 g ÷ 2.016 g/mol = 2.480 mol, which could make 2.480 × 2/3 = 1.653 mol NH₃. N₂ makes less, so it is limiting. 1.428 mol × 17.03 g/mol = 24.3 g NH₃.
N₂ is limiting: 0.7138 mol N₂ uses 3 × 0.7138 = 2.141 mol H₂ = 4.317 g H₂. Left over: 5.00 g − 4.32 g = 0.68 g H₂ (subtraction keeps two decimal places).

With equal masses, the lighter molecule gives more moles: 1 g of H₂ is 0.496 mol, while 1 g of O₂ is 0.0313 mol. Even though each O₂ needs two H₂, there are about 16 times more moles of H₂, so O₂ runs out first.
options: Right: equal masses give far fewer moles of the heavier O₂.
H₂ is needed in twice the moles, but there are about 16 times as many moles of H₂ present.
Equal masses of different substances hold different numbers of moles.
Size does not decide which runs out; the ratio of moles present to moles needed does.

why.correct: Put the unit you want on top and the unit you have on the bottom, with the coefficients as the numbers: 6 mol H₂O per 5 mol O₂.
options: Right: wanted over given, with the coefficients.
Inverts the ratio, so mol O₂ would not cancel.
Coefficients relate moles, not grams.
Ignores the coefficients 5 and 6 from the balanced equation.

why.correct: Weigh and dissolve; precipitate with a small excess of reagent; filter and rinse; dry to constant mass; then calculate.
A yield over 100% means the weighed "product" includes something else, such as water. Losing product or an incomplete reaction would lower the yield instead.
options: Right: water adds mass that is not product.
Spilled product is lost, so the actual yield is too low.
Lost product lowers the actual yield, so the percent would be below 100%.
An incomplete reaction makes less product, so the percent would be below 100%.

why.correct: The rough trial is a quick first run that overshoots; it is not used. Trials 1-3 agree closely: (39.67 + 39.68 + 39.66) mL ÷ 3 = 39.67 mL.
Moles NaOH = 0.1050 mol/L × 0.03967 L = 0.004165 mol. Mole ratio 1 : 1, so 0.004165 mol CH₃COOH. Molarity = 0.004165 mol ÷ 0.00500 L = 0.833 M (three significant figures, from 5.00 mL).

The NaOH needed depends on the moles of acid present, and adding water does not change that number. Only the volume of vinegar pipetted (5.00 mL) enters the calculation, so the water need not be measured precisely.
options: Right: dilution changes concentration, not moles of acid.
The water stays in the flask; it does not need to evaporate to have no effect.
Water does not use up hydroxide; if it did, the extra water would change the result.
The water is not used in the calculation at all; that is why "about 20 mL" is fine.

why.correct: Water left in the buret dilutes the titrant, so its real concentration is below 0.1050 M. More volume is needed for the same moles of acid. The calculation still uses 0.1050 M, so it counts too many moles of NaOH and the acid molarity comes out too high.
options: Right: a larger volume times the labeled molarity overstates the moles of base.
The diluted base still reacts with all the acid; it just takes more volume, which raises the calculated result.
The concentration of the solution in the buret drops, so more volume is used; the calculation uses the label concentration and the larger volume.
The water in the buret mixes with the NaOH, not the acid; the effect is a larger titrant volume.

why.correct: A faint pink that lasts shows the first slight excess of NaOH. Dark pink means many drops of excess base were added past that point, which is why the rough trial used 40.45 mL instead of about 39.67 mL.
options: Right: the deep color shows a large excess of base.
All trials used the same vinegar, measured with the same pipet.
The indicator was in the flask from the start; it changed color strongly because of the excess base.
At the end point the color is faint; dark pink means it went well past.

why.correct: Read at the bottom of the meniscus, at eye level. It sits a little more than halfway from 3.4 to 3.5, so 3.46 mL, with the last digit estimated.
27.81 mL − 3.46 mL = 24.35 mL. Both readings carry two decimal places, so the volume does too.
A measurement records every certain digit plus one estimated digit. The 0.1 mL marks make the tenths certain; the hundredths are estimated by eye.
options: Right: certain digits plus one estimated digit.
The last digit is an estimate, which is why it carries some uncertainty.
The precision of a reading depends on the instrument, not on the other values in the calculation.
The meniscus is a curved surface, not a layer of a set thickness; you read its lowest point.

why.correct: Reading the edge shifts each reading by the same small amount (the meniscus has the same shape both times). The volume is a difference, so a constant shift cancels. The habit is still wrong: reading the bottom of the meniscus at eye level avoids errors when the shapes differ.
options: Right: a constant offset in both readings cancels in final minus initial.
The top edge reads a slightly smaller number for both readings, so the difference barely changes.
Each reading shifts the same way, so the volume, a difference, is nearly unchanged.
Each reading is taken once; the error is a small shift, not a doubling.

why.correct: Moles HCl = 0.0985 mol/L × 0.02435 L = 0.002398 mol = moles OH⁻ (1 : 1). Molarity NaOH = 0.002398 mol ÷ 0.02000 L = 0.120 M, three significant figures from 0.0985 M.
Moles NaOH = 0.1000 mol/L × 0.03120 L = 0.003120 mol. × (1 mol H₂SO₄ / 2 mol NaOH) = 0.001560 mol H₂SO₄. ÷ 0.02500 L = 0.06240 M.
0.5106 g ÷ 204.22 g/mol = 0.002500 mol, which is also the moles of NaOH (1 : 1). 0.002500 mol ÷ 0.02487 L = 0.1005 M.

At the equivalence point the moles of titrant added match the analyte by the mole ratio. The end point is what you see, the indicator's color change. A well-chosen indicator makes them nearly the same.
options: Right: one is a stoichiometric point, the other an observation.
Neither depends on emptying the buret; titrations often use a fraction of it.
With a good indicator they nearly coincide, within about a drop.
Swaps the definitions: the color change is the end point.

why.correct: Rinse with titrant so it is not diluted, fill and clear the tip so trapped air is not counted as volume, read the starting volume, titrate slowly near the end, then read again.

An air bubble that escapes during the titration would be counted as delivered liquid. Washing drops of titrant from the flask wall into the solution with distilled water adds no moles and lets all the titrant react.
options: Right: a bubble that leaves the tip during the run would add false volume.
Water left in the buret dilutes the titrant; the last rinse should be with titrant.
Right: distilled water adds no acid or base, and it washes stray drops into the reaction.
Reading from above gives a parallax error; read at eye level.

why.correct: The titrant's concentration changes the volume needed, not the moles. The answer for the acid stays the same.

variables.name: Volume of NaOH needed to reach the end point
variables.why: The more concentrated base delivers the same moles in half the volume.

variables.name: Moles of NaOH needed to reach the end point
variables.why: The moles of acid are unchanged, so the same moles of base are needed (1 : 1).

variables.name: Calculated molarity of acetic acid
variables.why: Half the volume times twice the molarity gives the same moles, so the result is the same.

variables.name: Moles of acetic acid in the 5.00 mL sample
variables.why: The sample is the same vinegar and the same pipetted volume.

why.correct: In reaction 1 two solutions are mixed and an insoluble solid, PbCl₂(s), forms from ions that were dissolved.
options: Right: two solutions give an insoluble solid.
Reaction 2 makes a gas from a metal and acid; no solid forms from the solutions.
Reaction 3 makes water and a soluble salt; every product stays dissolved or is liquid water.
Reaction 5 is one substance breaking into two; no solid forms.

why.correct: Reaction 2: Mg metal becomes Mg²⁺ and H⁺ becomes H₂. Reaction 5: oxygen in H₂O₂ ends up partly as O₂. In reactions 1 and 3, every ion keeps its charge; ions change partners or an H⁺ moves. (Reaction 4, a combustion, also transfers electrons.)
options: In reaction 1 the ions Pb²⁺, NO₃⁻, Na⁺ and Cl⁻ keep their charges; they only change partners, so no electrons move.
Right: neutral Mg atoms become Mg²⁺ ions and H⁺ ions become neutral H₂.
In reaction 3 an H⁺ moves from HNO₃ to OH⁻; no element changes from uncombined to combined, so no electrons move.
Right: some oxygen leaves the compound as the element O₂.

why.correct: HNO₃ and KOH are fully ionized in water, and K⁺ and NO₃⁻ are spectators. What changes is an H⁺ joining an OH⁻ to make water: the acid-base reaction in its simplest form.
options: Right: only H⁺ and OH⁻ change.
KNO₃(aq) is just the spectator ions dissolved; nothing changes there.
Unbalanced (K⁺ appears from nowhere) and it keeps a spectator.
KOH is a soluble ionic compound, so it is written as K⁺ and OH⁻, and K⁺ is a spectator.

why.correct: Use the clue for electron transfer: an element uncombined on one side and combined on the other. Oxygen is the free element O₂ before and part of the compounds CO₂ and H₂O after, so electrons have moved. That is true of every combustion.
options: Right: oxygen goes from the free element to compounds, so electrons move.
Many processes give off heat without electron transfer, such as an acid neutralizing a base; heat and light are not the test.
Forming a gas says nothing about electrons; reaction 2 makes a gas by electron transfer, but boiling makes gas with none.
Oxygen already in ethanol stays combined; the clue is the O₂ that starts uncombined.

why.correct: 1.261 g H₂O × (1 mol H₂O / 18.02 g) × (2 mol H / 1 mol H₂O) = 0.1400 mol H. All the hydrogen in the water came from the hydrocarbon.
Ratio H : C = 0.1400 ÷ 0.06001 = 2.333, which is 7/3. So the smallest whole-number ratio is C₃H₇ (multiply 1 : 2.333 by 3).
options: Rounds 2.333 down to 2; a ratio this far from a whole number has to be multiplied, not rounded.
Uses moles of water (0.0700) instead of moles of H atoms, so the hydrogen count is halved.
C₃H₈ would need H : C = 2.667, which the data do not give.

why.correct: 0.06001 mol × 12.01 g/mol = 0.7207 g C; 0.1400 mol × 1.008 g/mol = 0.1411 g H. Total 0.8618 g, which matches the 0.8617 g sample within rounding, so all the mass is C and H.
C₃H₇ has a formula mass of about 43 g/mol, so the molecule is twice that: C₆H₁₄. 2C₆H₁₄ gives 12 CO₂ and 14 H₂O, which hold 24 + 14 = 38 O, so 19 O₂.
options: Right: the molecular formula is C₆H₁₄ and every atom balances.
Uses the empirical formula as if it were the molecule (43 g/mol, not 86 g/mol), and hydrogen does not balance: 7 H on the left, 8 on the right.
Carbon and hydrogen balance, but oxygen does not: 38 O on the left and 6 × 2 + 7 = 19 O on the right. 19 O₂ goes with two C₆H₁₄.
Gives carbon monoxide, which forms only when oxygen is short; with excess oxygen the product is CO₂.

why.correct: Two Mg atoms and four H⁺ ions were used; two Mg²⁺ ions and two H₂ molecules formed. That is a 1 : 2 : 1 : 1 ratio. Cl⁻ is unchanged (4 before, 4 after), so it is a spectator.
options: Right: atoms and charge balance (+2 each side) and Cl⁻ is left out.
This is the molecular equation; it keeps the spectator chloride ions.
Unbalanced in atoms and charge, and hydrogen forms H₂ molecules, not single atoms.
No solid MgCl₂ forms; the Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions stay dissolved in the After box.

why.correct: H⁺ ran out (4 before, 0 after). One Mg atom is left, so magnesium was in excess.
options: Right: the reactant used up is H⁺.
Fewer particles does not mean limiting: each Mg needs two H⁺, and H⁺ ran out first.
A spectator ion is not a reactant, so it cannot be limiting.
A reactant that is left over is in excess, not limiting.

why.correct: Two Mg atoms each lost two electrons (Mg → Mg²⁺): 4 electrons. Four H⁺ ions each gained one electron to form two H₂: 4 electrons. Electrons lost equal electrons gained.
Electrons pass from Mg atoms to H⁺ ions: magnesium becomes Mg²⁺ and the hydrogen ions become H₂. No proton is handed to a base, no solid forms from solution and nothing burns in oxygen.
options: H⁺ is not passed to a base that keeps it; each H⁺ gains an electron from magnesium and leaves as H₂ gas.
Right: neutral Mg becomes Mg²⁺ and H⁺ becomes neutral H₂.
No insoluble solid forms; magnesium dissolves rather than precipitates.
Combustion is a reaction with O₂; there is no oxygen gas here.

why.correct: 2C₄H₁₀ + 13O₂ → 8CO₂ + 10H₂O. The right side has 16 + 10 = 26 O atoms, so 13 O₂. Doubling the butane avoids the fraction 13/2.
options: Right: 2C₄H₁₀ + 13O₂ → 8CO₂ + 10H₂O.
Balances 1 C₄H₁₀ but leaves a fraction; equations use whole numbers, so double everything.
Adds the product coefficients for one butane (4 CO₂ + 5 H₂O = 9); count oxygen atoms, not molecules, and clear the fraction.
That is the number of O atoms, not O₂ molecules.

why.correct: With too little oxygen, carbon ends up as carbon monoxide instead of carbon dioxide: incomplete combustion. CO is colorless, odorless and toxic.
options: Right: incomplete combustion, with too little O₂, makes CO.
This is complete combustion, which needs plenty of oxygen; its products are not the toxic gas.
Methane does not simply break apart in a furnace flame without oxygen being involved.
Making methanol needs special conditions and is not what happens in a furnace.

why.correct: The new combination Ca²⁺ with CO₃²⁻ is insoluble, so it precipitates. K⁺ and Cl⁻ stay dissolved as spectators.
options: Right: the insoluble combination precipitates.
Soluble starting compounds can still make an insoluble product when their ions meet new partners.
Potassium chloride is soluble, so its ions stay dissolved.
Carbonate gives off CO₂ when an acid is added, not in plain water with calcium ions.

why.correct: Electrons move when an element goes from uncombined to combined or the reverse. Oxygen leaves KClO₃ as the element O₂; sodium and chlorine start as elements and end as Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in NaCl. Breaking CaCO₃ into two compounds and a precipitation keep every ion's charge.
options: One compound breaks into two compounds. No element is uncombined on either side: calcium stays Ca²⁺ and carbon stays bonded to oxygen, so no electrons move.
Right: oxygen in the compound KClO₃ becomes the free element O₂.
Right: neutral Na atoms become Na⁺ and Cl₂ becomes Cl⁻.
The ions only change partners and keep their charges, so this precipitation moves no electrons.

why.correct: Water gives up an H⁺ (becoming OH⁻) and ammonia accepts it (becoming NH₄⁺). The proton donor on the reactant side is water.
options: Right: water donates the proton and becomes OH⁻.
Ammonia gains an H⁺, so it is the base (proton acceptor).
NH₄⁺ is a product: the conjugate acid formed when ammonia accepts the proton.
OH⁻ is a product: what is left of water after it donates a proton.

why.correct: In reaction 1, water accepts the proton from HF and becomes H₃O⁺, so it is a base there. In reaction 2 water donates a proton (acid). In reaction 3 water is a product, and in reaction 4 it does not appear.
options: Right: water accepts H⁺ from HF and becomes hydronium.
In reaction 2 water gives an H⁺ to ammonia, so it is the acid.
Water is formed in reaction 3 (when OH⁻ gains a proton); it is not a reactant there.
Water is not one of the reacting species in reaction 4.

why.correct: Remove one H⁺ from HCO₃⁻ and you get CO₃²⁻; the charge drops by one. They differ by exactly one proton, so they are a conjugate pair.
options: Right: HCO₃⁻ minus H⁺ is CO₃²⁻.
H₂CO₃ has one more H⁺, so it is the conjugate acid of HCO₃⁻.
OH⁻ is the base that takes the proton; its conjugate acid is H₂O.
Water is the conjugate acid of OH⁻, not related to HCO₃⁻ by one proton.

why.correct: In reaction 3 HCO₃⁻ donates a proton to OH⁻. It also has a site to accept one (giving H₂CO₃). A species that can do either is amphoteric, like water.
options: Right: it can donate or accept a proton.
A negative charge does not decide; in reaction 3 HCO₃⁻ donates a proton, acting as an acid.
It does have an H to give, but it can also accept a proton on an oxygen lone pair, forming H₂CO₃.
It changes (it loses H⁺), so it is not a spectator.

why.correct: A conjugate pair differs by one H⁺. NH₃ gains a proton to become NH₄⁺. The other pair is CH₃COOH and CH₃COO⁻.
options: Right: they differ by exactly one H⁺.
These are the acid and base that react with each other, not a conjugate pair.
These are the two products: the conjugate base of one pair and the conjugate acid of the other.
Both are proton donors from different pairs; they do not differ by one H⁺.

why.correct: Each HCl molecule gives its H⁺ to a water molecule. The diagram shows only H₃O⁺ and Cl⁻ afterward, with no HCl molecules left.
options: Right: a proton moves from HCl to water.
The diagram shows ions, not neutral H and Cl atoms.
No hydrogen gas forms; the H ends up in hydronium.
If HCl simply dissolved, the right box would show HCl molecules, but it shows none.

why.correct: Water takes the H⁺ and becomes H₃O⁺, so water is the Brønsted-Lowry base.
options: Right: water accepts the proton.
HCl gives the proton away, so it is the acid.
Cl⁻ is a product, the conjugate base of HCl.
H₃O⁺ is a product, the conjugate acid of water.

why.correct: Pure HCl is made of neutral molecules, so nothing carries charge. In water, the proton transfer makes H₃O⁺ and Cl⁻ ions that move through the solution and conduct.
options: Right: the reaction with water creates mobile ions.
Pure water conducts very poorly; the ions from HCl are what make the solution conduct.
Pure HCl is molecular, not ionic, which is why it does not conduct.
Neutral atoms carry no charge; the diagram shows ions.

why.correct: Add one H⁺: the formula gains an H and the charge rises by one, from 2− to 1−, giving H₂PO₄⁻.
options: Right: one more H⁺, charge 2− becomes 1−.
That is the conjugate base, with one H⁺ removed.
That adds two protons, not one.
Adds an H but forgets that the proton's + charge changes 2− to 1−.

why.correct: Removing H⁺ removes one hydrogen and one positive charge: HF (0) → F⁻ (1−), NH₄⁺ (1+) → NH₃ (0).
options: Right: one H and one positive charge leave together.
Losing a positive charge lowers the overall charge; it does not raise it.
A conjugate base differs by one H⁺, not by an added OH.
The proton carries a + charge, so removing it changes the charge.

why.correct: Ammonia has no OH, yet it accepts a proton from HCl, so it is a base. The Brønsted-Lowry definition (proton acceptor) covers it; "contains OH" does not.
options: Right: NH₃ acts as a base without containing OH.
Here the base contains OH, so this reaction fits the narrow definition.
Here too the base is a hydroxide, which fits the narrow definition.
The base is again a hydroxide, so this does not test the definition.

why.correct: An amphoteric species must have an H to give and a site to take one. Water can become OH⁻ or H₃O⁺; HSO₄⁻ can become SO₄²⁻ or H₂SO₄.
options: Right: water can lose or gain H⁺.
Right: HSO₄⁻ has an H to give and can also accept one.
Cl⁻ has no hydrogen, so it cannot donate a proton.
NH₄⁺ can donate a proton but has no lone pair left to accept another.

why.correct: H⁺ is a lone proton with an intense positive charge in a tiny space. It bonds at once to a lone pair on a water oxygen, giving hydronium. H⁺(aq) is shorthand for it.
options: Right: the proton bonds to a lone pair on water.
A proton is far smaller than any atom; size is not the reason.
Hydronium forms at room temperature whenever an acid gives protons to water; it is what H⁺(aq) stands for.
Water is a reactant (proton acceptor) here, not a spectator.

why.correct: The change is H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l). Hydroxide is used up, water forms, and the spectators follow their sources.

variables.name: Number of OH⁻ ions in the beaker
variables.why: Each H⁺ added combines with an OH⁻ to form water.

variables.name: Number of Na⁺ ions in the beaker
variables.why: Na⁺ is a spectator; none is added or removed.

variables.name: Number of Cl⁻ ions in the beaker
variables.why: Each portion of HCl adds chloride ions, which stay dissolved as spectators.

variables.name: Number of water molecules in the beaker
variables.why: Water is a product of H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O, and the acid solution also adds water.

why.correct: Copper atoms lose 2 electrons each (Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻) and each Ag⁺ gains 1 (Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag). Two Ag⁺ are needed per Cu so electrons lost equal electrons gained; charge is +2 on both sides.
options: Right: 2 electrons lost and 2 gained; atoms and charge balance.
Atoms balance, but charge does not (+1 left, +2 right): electrons lost (2) do not equal electrons gained (1).
This is the reverse; the table shows silver metal does not react with Cu²⁺.
Silver metal is written as Ag(s); it does not form Ag₂ units.

why.correct: Magnesium reacts with every other metal ion, so it gives electrons to all of them. Silver reacts with none, so it gives up electrons least readily. Order: Mg > Zn > Cu > Ag.
options: Right: Mg gives electrons to Cu²⁺, Zn²⁺ and Ag⁺.
Zinc reacts with Cu²⁺ and Ag⁺ but not Mg²⁺, so magnesium gives up electrons more readily.
Copper reacts only with Ag⁺.
Silver reacts with none of the solutions, so it loses electrons least readily.

why.correct: Cu²⁺ gains electrons (it is reduced to Cu), and by taking electrons it causes zinc to be oxidized. The species that is reduced is the oxidizing agent.
options: Right: Cu²⁺ is reduced, so it is the oxidizing agent.
Zinc loses electrons; it is oxidized, so it is the reducing agent.
Zn²⁺ is a product, formed when zinc is oxidized.
Copper metal is a product, formed when Cu²⁺ is reduced.

why.correct: Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s): zinc dissolves, copper ions leave the solution as metal, and nitrate stays put.

variables.name: Mass of the zinc strip, not counting the copper coating
variables.why: Zinc atoms are oxidized to Zn²⁺ ions and leave the strip.

variables.name: Intensity of the blue color of the solution
variables.why: Blue Cu²⁺ ions are reduced to copper metal and leave the solution.

variables.name: Number of nitrate ions in solution
variables.why: Nitrate is a spectator ion; it does not react.

variables.name: Number of Zn²⁺ ions in solution
variables.why: Each zinc atom oxidized adds one Zn²⁺ ion.

why.correct: Oxygen is −2, so 4 O contribute −8. The sum must equal the ion's charge, −1: Mn + (−8) = −1, so Mn = +7.
The oxidation number of Mn falls from +7 to +2, a gain of 5 electrons. That matches the 5 Fe²⁺ each losing 1 electron (Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺).
options: Right: +7 to +2 is a change of 5.
Uses the starting oxidation number alone; the change is what counts.
Uses the final oxidation number alone; the change is 7 − 2.
The charge of the ion is not the number of electrons transferred.

why.correct: Before the end point every drop of purple MnO₄⁻ is reduced to almost colorless Mn²⁺. Once all the Fe²⁺ is used, the next drop of MnO₄⁻ stays, coloring the solution pale pink.
options: Right: the titrant acts as its own indicator.
Fe³⁺ is pale yellow in this solution, not purple; the color at the end comes from unreacted MnO₄⁻.
These reactions do not glow; the color change is from leftover titrant.
The acid is there to supply H⁺ for the reaction; it does not change color.

why.correct: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ raises iron's oxidation number by one: iron loses an electron and is oxidized, so Fe²⁺ is the reducing agent. Manganese is reduced; H and O keep their oxidation numbers (+1 and −2).
options: Right: the species oxidized is the reducing agent.
MnO₄⁻ gains electrons (Mn +7 → +2), so it is reduced and is the oxidizing agent.
Hydrogen is +1 in H⁺ and +1 in H₂O; its oxidation number does not change.
Oxygen is −2 in MnO₄⁻ and −2 in H₂O; it is neither oxidized nor reduced.

why.correct: 2 H at +1 give +2; 4 O at −2 give −8. The compound is neutral: 2 + S − 8 = 0, so S = +6.
options: Right: +2 + S − 8 = 0.
That is sulfur in H₂SO₃ or SO₂, which hold less oxygen; in H₂SO₄ the four O at −2 give −8, so S is +6.
That is sulfur in a sulfide ion or H₂S, where S is bonded to no oxygen.
Ignores the hydrogens: S − 8 = 0 would mean no H atoms.

why.correct: In the first, H goes from 0 to +1 and O from 0 to −2. In the third, Fe goes from +3 to 0 and C from +2 to +4. In the precipitation and acid-base reactions no oxidation number changes.
options: Right: both elements change oxidation number.
Every ion keeps its charge; ions only change partners, so no electrons move.
Right: iron is reduced and carbon is oxidized.
An H⁺ moves, not electrons; all oxidation numbers stay the same.

why.correct: Make electrons lost equal electrons gained: the least common multiple of 3 and 2 is 6. Double the aluminum half-reaction (6e⁻ lost) and triple the copper one (6e⁻ gained), then add; the electrons cancel. Charge: +6 on each side.

why.correct: An agent causes the change in something else. The oxidizing agent oxidizes another substance by taking its electrons, so the agent gains electrons and is reduced.
options: Right: the oxidizing agent is reduced.
The name describes what it does to the other reactant, not what happens to it.
Many redox reactions have no oxygen, such as Zn + Cu²⁺; the oxidizing agent there is Cu²⁺.
With or without oxygen gas, the oxidizing agent is the species reduced.

Nickel gives electrons to Cu²⁺, so it loses electrons more readily than copper. It does not give electrons to Zn²⁺, so it loses them less readily than zinc. It fits between Zn and Cu.
options: Right: more readily than Cu, less readily than Zn.
If nickel were above magnesium, it would also reduce Zn²⁺, which it does not.
If nickel were below copper, it could not reduce Cu²⁺, but it does.
A metal below silver would not reduce Cu²⁺; nickel does.
